definition: Not influenced by any personal gain or loss, and so able to judge fairly.
example: The study was checked by a disinterested scientist whose funding did not depend on the result.
nuance: Disinterested means having nothing to gain from the outcome; uninterested means bored, and careful writers keep the two apart.
prompt: Two neighbors need someone to settle their argument over where a shared fence belongs.
options: They hired a disinterested surveyor, who knew neither family, to mark the property line.
They picked the disinterested surveyor because he owned the lot on one side.
The disinterested neighbor yawned and wandered off before anyone arrived.
The disinterested neighbor shouted that the fence was ugly and the family next door was even worse.
reasons: A stranger with nothing to win or lose on either side is exactly the fair referee needed.
Owning one of the lots gives him a stake, which is the opposite of being impartial.
Yawning shows boredom; that calls for uninterested, not a word about fairness.
Open hostility toward one side is strong bias, not neutral judgment.

practice.prompt: A middle school needs someone to judge its annual science fair.
options: The coach's daughter had entered, so he made a perfectly disinterested judge.
The judge seemed disinterested, checking the clock every few minutes and skipping half of the posters.
A disinterested judge gave top marks to projects built by his own former students.
The principal invited a disinterested chemist from another town with no relatives in the contest.
reasons: A parent of a contestant has a personal stake and cannot count as neutral.
Watching the clock signals boredom, which is what uninterested describes.
Rewarding his own students shows favoritism, the reverse of fairness.
An outsider with no family competing has no reason to favor any project.
